![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/a53074660204fdd4fd62575ef8db80a3b04144ef7b9e18d98c60fbbe9a480ee3.png)

The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there are two critical points: 

$\,$ $x=-1\,$ and $\,x=1$

Also, we have the following: 

- If ${f}^{′}(x)>0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

- If ${f}^{′}(x)<0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x):$

- First, we draw the critical points. We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical lines $x=-1$ and $x=1.$ Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-1,1),$ the point at $x=1$ must be higher than the point at $x=-1,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/12e6a8036759b8bbcc2f4fbe4ae7f4f7e18278de65fbdc0faa99c919f7234284.png)

- Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

- Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $↘$ on $(-\infty ,-1)$ and is increasing $↗$ on $(-1,1)$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes up to the left and the right of $x=-1.$

- Since $f(x)$ is increasing $↗$ on $(-1,1)$ and is decreasing $↘$ on $(1,\infty )$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes down to the left and the right of $x=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/38f1c92810a3311ed939a54ac2856cb7ada111dbf24528785f80bd5f9ca49c84.png)

- Finally, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x):$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14200695/assets/7921a107b33a9b9bdc3df8dec418828f4cd5de2d89a9e7ab41845b0c64bbb653.png)

**Note:** The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
